chapter: The jazz war with Leonard Feather
title: Communist charges, politics and the tapped Jazz Record phone
summary: DeMichael recalls Metronome implying Hodes was a Communist. Hodes explains his working-class Democrat views and the tapped Jazz Record phone in the wartime Village.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Politics, race and the state of the country

blocks.x: I remember reading something -- I think it was Leonard who wrote it. I think it was in Metronome. Either accusing you or by implication accusing you of being Communist because you played for a labor union that was Communist-dominated -- a guild, newspaper guild or something like that.
Well, Ralph Toledano wrote a -- some few things for us, and we knew that he was to the right of the

right, but he also attracted people who were to the left of the left, to write for us. I never asked them what their politics was. My record was very clear that I was from the wrong side of the tracks, according to wealth, I was a working man. That's where my feelings lie, and so I was going to vote Democrat every time I could. I never voted Socialist, but I figured the Demmies were the best of two evils and they were better for the working class. They could look that record up. In fact, our phone was tapped for a long time.

The Jazz Record phone was tapped, because -- well, the government, no doubt because of the people -- at that time, the Village was a hotbed of kids that were becoming radically -- who were radically-inclined Russian lovers, because after all, --
We were in the war. We were buddy-buddy.
